definition: Deciding in-between count and placement by repeatedly adding drawings or keys "until it looks right," with no grounding in a measured reference or a stated rule — explicitly named and warned against for a beginner, but reframed as a legitimate, fast shortcut once an animator has enough experience to judge correctly by instinct.
purpose: Name a specific, common workflow mistake so it can be recognized and avoided by someone without the experience to safely skip a grounded timing method — and to state honestly that the same workflow stops being a mistake once real judgement backs it.
visible_effect: No single visible signature — the failure mode is in the AUTHORING PROCESS (guessing and iterating without a reference), not a specific pose or curve shape, so its symptom is whatever an ungrounded guess happens to produce: sometimes fine, sometimes wrong, inconsistently.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: For a beginner, produces inconsistent, unreliable results because there is no way to tell whether an iteration "looks right" for a principled reason or by accident; for an expert, the same fast iteration is reliable because their instinct has already internalized what a grounded method would have measured anyway.
physical_interpretation: None directly — a judgement and workflow distinction, not a physical property of the resulting motion.
use_cases: a simple, well-understood movement for an animator experienced enough to time it correctly on instinct, where a full stopwatch or recording pass would be redundant effort
a rapid rough/preview pass where precision does not yet matter and will be revisited later with a grounded method
non_use_cases: a beginner or anyone without demonstrated instinct for the specific type of movement being timed — the video is explicit that this is the wrong place to start

a complex, multi-beat action where even an experienced animator would benefit from a grounded reference — the video's own example uses the recording method specifically because that cut "is a bit on the complex side"
interactions: Physical reference timing method — this is the exact failure mode that method exists to prevent for anyone not yet experienced enough to skip it; the two entries describe the same decision from opposite ends of the experience curve

Timing — the existing card already treats timing as the most semantically loaded of the twelve principles; this entry names the specific process failure that produces an unreliably loaded result rather than a deliberately chosen one
Certainty / evidence (Part 13) — vibe timing is the animation-authoring equivalent of an unevidenced claim: it may happen to be correct, but nothing about the process itself justifies trusting it
cadence_representation: Not directly represented as a named anti-pattern, but closely related to a standing constraint on this build: the user's own stated requirement for Cadence is "exact (computed, never estimated)" — this entry is the human-animator-workflow version of exactly the failure that constraint exists to rule out. Nothing in Cadence currently distinguishes a grounded key placement from an ungrounded one; every key is stored identically regardless of how its value was decided.
detection_and_measurement_methods: None, and likely none possible: whether a given key placement was "vibed" or grounded in a reference is a fact about the AUTHORING PROCESS, not something recoverable from the resulting project data alone.
failure_modes: a beginner repeatedly guessing in-between placement with no reference, producing inconsistent results with no principled way to diagnose why a given attempt felt wrong
an experienced animator over-trusting instinct on a movement type they do NOT actually have deep experience with, applying the "expert exception" where it does not actually apply
roblox_considerations: None specific — a pure authoring-workflow concept independent of the target engine.
examples: explicitly named and warned against for beginners early in the video ("you really shouldn't be guessing at timing when you are a beginner... don't do it") (video 9 @ 5:01–5:27)

the same animator later applying what he calls the same "vibe timing" by name to a simple head-lift action, explicitly because years of experience let him place the exact same kind of spacing diagram from instinct rather than needing a fresh measurement (video 9 @ 11:36–13:22)
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/13QIh7vsCpQ @ 5:01–5:27 and 11:36–13:22 — Dong Chang names "vibe timing" explicitly in both the warning and the later expert-exception passage, using the same term deliberately in both places; experimental until validated
